opening: Russia and Ukraine agreed a large prisoner exchange as the Abu Dhabi talks ended, with US envoys heading to Moscow. Iran denied any talks and kept Hormuz shut, Spain held its first general strike since 2012, and France blamed Iran for supermarket sabotage.

stories.title: The Abu Dhabi talks end with Russia and Ukraine agreeing to a large prisoner exchange, as US envoys head to Moscow to see Putin
stories.region: Europe · Ukraine, Russia · Middle East · UAE
stories.body: The first three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States since February ended on Wednesday after a short second session in Abu Dhabi. Both chief negotiators, Vladimir Medinsky for Russia and Rustem Umerov for Ukraine, confirmed a large exchange of prisoners, with the numbers to be settled on Thursday. Medinsky said European security was the central subject and that Russia would recover what it calls its land one way or another. The US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Vladimir Putin.
stories.whatChanged: The round produced its first concrete result, an agreed prisoner exchange, but no visible movement on territory, and the mediators’ next step is a meeting with Putin himself.
stories.whyMatters: An exchange on this scale would be one of the largest of the war and the first tangible result since talks stalled in February. But Moscow’s public line on land leaves the central dispute where it was, and Russia is now framing any deal as part of a wider bargain over European security.
stories.uncertainty: The size and timing of the exchange are not final. On Tuesday an unnamed US official spoke of private flexibility on territory, but Medinsky’s remarks after the talks point the other way. No date has been set for another three-way round.
stories.watchNext: The final numbers for the exchange on Thursday, November 12, the envoys’ meeting with Putin in Moscow and then with Zelensky in Dublin, and whether a further round is scheduled.
keyFacts: The talks ran on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi, the first three-way round since Geneva in February
Zelensky said an exchange of 1,000 or 1,500 prisoners on each side was being discussed
Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 163 drones and several missiles before the second day of talks
Six large electricity substations were hit in the Vinnytsia, Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr and Cherkasy regions
A Ukrainian drone attack set fire to Russia’s Ust-Luga oil export port, injuring three workers, the regional governor said

report.heading: What was agreed
paragraphs: The first day of talks on Tuesday lasted about four hours by the Associated Press’s account, and longer by Russian state media’s. The second day, on Wednesday, ran for a little under two hours before the delegations broke up. Kushner described the planned exchange as the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, and both Medinsky and Umerov confirmed it. The Associated Press reported that the numbers would be finalised on Thursday.

Zelensky said the first day covered prisoners of war, civilians held in captivity, children taken from Ukraine and security guarantees, and called it constructive. The US envoys and European officials also issued a joint statement with Ukraine on respecting its sovereignty and on guarantees, ABC News reported.

report.heading: Moscow’s line
paragraphs: Speaking after the talks, Medinsky said security in Europe had to be dealt with as a whole rather than patched up, and that Russia had raised its 2021 proposals, including an end to NATO’s expansion. He said Ukraine could join the European Union but not NATO, that Russia held no talks with the Europeans in Abu Dhabi, and he praised the American mediators. The Kremlin said it would give no details until the delegation had reported to Putin.

Zelensky said Putin’s refusal of a ceasefire before a long-term settlement showed he did not want to end the war. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in Paris, called the talks very productive but said a breakthrough would take time.

report.heading: Strikes around the talks
paragraphs: The fighting did not pause. Ukraine’s air force said it brought down 130 drones and 14 Banderol missiles overnight, with impacts at 17 places, and parts of Kryvyi Rih lost power and heating. People were injured in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv and Zhytomyr. Russia said it downed more than 600 Ukrainian drones across 22 regions; two people were killed in the Smolensk region, and more than 20 Russian airports briefly restricted flights.

report.heading: What comes next
paragraphs: Witkoff and Kushner are due in Moscow on Thursday and then in Dublin to see Zelensky. Positions remain far apart: Putin wants Ukraine to leave the four regions Russia claims, while Kyiv wants a ceasefire first.

stories.title: Iran says there are no talks with Washington and the Strait of Hormuz stays shut, as tankers are hit in UAE waters
stories.body: A day after President Trump said there was a good chance of a deal, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called reports of negotiations a lie and said the Strait of Hormuz would stay closed until Iran’s conditions were met. Those include lifting sanctions and the US naval blockade, releasing frozen assets and paying reparations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected reparations and said the blockade meant major combat was not needed for now. On Tuesday an attack damaged a vessel of the UAE’s state oil shipping company in UAE waters.
stories.whatChanged: Tehran flatly denied that talks exist and set out its price for reopening the strait, Washington ruled out reparations, and attacks on shipping continued despite the pause in US strikes.
stories.whyMatters: Oil prices have fallen to two-month lows on hopes of peace, yet the strait is still closed and ships are still being hit. Markets are betting on a deal that the two governments do not yet describe in the same way.
stories.uncertainty: No one has claimed the attacks on ships, and it is unclear whether three burning tankers reported by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are the same incidents reported by the UAE and Oman. Iran’s full list of conditions has not been published.
stories.watchNext: Whether either side confirms contacts through Qatar or other mediators, further attacks on Gulf shipping, and oil prices as traders weigh American optimism against Iranian denials.
keyFacts: Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Hormuz could reopen within two days of Iran’s demands being met
Four crew were injured when a projectile hit the tanker Fujairah Energy between Abu Dhabi and Dubai, India’s shipping minister said
The International Maritime Organization counts about 130 incidents involving ships since late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed
Rubio told G7 ministers in Paris that sanctions and the blockade make major combat unnecessary for now

report.heading: Two different stories
paragraphs: President Trump told reporters at the White House on Tuesday that Tehran was talking very politely and that a deal had a good chance, while saying the United States remained ready to strike. In Tehran, Rezaei said no negotiations were taking place, dismissed reports of a meeting in Qatar and called the American response to Iran’s conditions inadequate and deceptive. Araghchi also denied a reported meeting between Rezaei and Vice President JD Vance.

Iran’s conditions, as described by its officials, include an end to sanctions and the blockade, the release of frozen assets, reparations and an end to fighting on all fronts, particularly Israel’s strikes in Lebanon.

report.heading: Washington’s position
paragraphs: At the G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris, Rubio said the United States would keep imposing heavy economic costs and that reparations were out of the question, accusing Iran of wanting cash handouts. He said no breakthrough was close and described Iran’s terms as not serious.

report.heading: Attacks at sea
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi’s state shipping company, ADNOC Logistics and Services, said one of its vessels was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters on Tuesday, without naming the ship. India’s shipping minister said on Wednesday that the Liberian-flagged supertanker Fujairah Energy, with six Indians among its 22 crew, was struck between Abu Dhabi and Dubai and four crew were hurt; it has not been officially confirmed that this is the same ship. Britain’s maritime trade agency separately reported a tanker hit by an unknown projectile off Oman, and the Revolutionary Guards said three tankers were on fire in the strait.
Reuters reported that oil prices hit two-month lows on Tuesday even as attacks continued. The International Maritime Organization counts about 130 incidents since late February.

stories.title: The House shelves Thomas Massie’s impeachment articles against Pete Hegseth, who calls them a political spectacle
stories.body: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to send Representative Thomas Massie’s eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, which in practice ends them in the current Congress. Massie was the only Republican to oppose the move, and every Democrat joined him. Earlier, at his first Pentagon news conference since May, Hegseth called the effort a spectacle driven by a defeated congressman and said he stood behind every operation. Democrats, who take control of the House in January, promise their own investigations.
stories.whatChanged: A day after Massie forced the issue, the Republican majority set the impeachment aside, and Hegseth answered the charges in public for the first time.
stories.whyMatters: The articles concern the war with Iran, the strikes on alleged drug boats and the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro. The vote ends the challenge in this Congress but leaves those operations to a Democratic House that will have subpoena power from January.
stories.uncertainty: Democrats have not said which investigations they will open or when. The casualty figures in the articles are Massie’s own and have not been independently established.
stories.watchNext: A December 11 deadline to fund the government during the lame-duck session, and the new Congress in January, when Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become Speaker.
keyFacts: The House voted 211 to 204 on November 10 to refer the articles to the Judiciary Committee
Massie filed a 34-page privileged resolution with eight articles on November 9
The articles cite boat strikes in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific that killed 243 people
It was Hegseth’s first Pentagon news conference since May

report.heading: The vote
paragraphs: Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger, used a privileged resolution, which forces the House to act within two legislative days. He had first introduced the articles in September, but a vote stalled when the House adjourned before the midterms. On Tuesday the Republican majority voted to refer them to committee, a step that effectively kills them before the new Congress begins. Speaker Mike Johnson said the House would dispense with what he called a gambit.

report.heading: What the articles allege
paragraphs: The articles accuse Hegseth of waging war on Iran without a declaration or authorisation from Congress, in breach of the War Powers Resolution, and cite a strike on an elementary school. They also cite strikes on boats alleged to be smuggling drugs, retaliation against Senator Mark Kelly, a Yemen operation and the raid that captured Maduro, which Massie calls a kidnapping.

report.heading: Hegseth’s answer
paragraphs: Hegseth said no defence secretary had ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations and called the vote a farce. He said the effort was driven by ego and resentment and that he would carry out the same operations again. A Pentagon spokesman said he was fully committed to serving until the end of Trump’s term. Massie said every member would now have to go on record. Jeffries, the Democratic leader, said Democrats would drive Hegseth from office.

report.heading: What comes next
paragraphs: The lame-duck Congress, which returned on November 9, has until December 11 to pass a short-term funding bill to avoid a shutdown. Democrats take over the House in January after their midterm gains.

stories.title: Spain holds its first general strike in 14 years over wages, housing and prices, less than three weeks before a snap election
stories.body: Spain’s two biggest unions, CCOO and UGT, began a 24-hour general strike at midnight on Wednesday under the banner of wages, housing and prices, their first since 2012. The unions say millions of workers joined, with public transport disrupted and many shops and factories shut. Burning tyres blocked roads in Barcelona, and there were scuffles with police near Madrid’s wholesale market. Rents have nearly doubled in a decade, and the Bank of Spain estimates the country is 750,000 homes short. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election for November 29.
stories.whatChanged: Months of protest over housing became a nationwide stoppage, putting the cost of living at the centre of an election campaign Sánchez called after failing to pass housing measures.
stories.whyMatters: Housing costs have become one of Europe’s sharpest political pressures. The strike tests whether anger over rents translates into votes, with the conservative People’s Party leading the polls ahead of the November 29 election.
stories.uncertainty: Participation figures come from the unions, and no independent count was available by our cutoff. The People’s Party, Vox and business groups describe the strike as an election protest rather than a labour dispute.
stories.watchNext: Official figures on the strike’s reach, the campaign’s housing pledges, and the election on Sunday, November 29.
keyFacts: The strike runs for 24 hours from midnight on November 11
It is the first general strike called by CCOO and UGT since 2012
The unions say about 90 percent of workers in the car and port sectors stopped
The Bank of Spain estimates a shortfall of 750,000 homes
The snap general election is on November 29

report.heading: The stoppage
paragraphs: The strike began at midnight and was due to last a full day. The unions said around nine in ten workers in the car industry and the ports had stopped, while public transport was disrupted and many shops and factories stayed closed. Pickets set burning tyres across roads in Barcelona, and there were scuffles with police near Madrid’s central wholesale market.

report.heading: Why now
paragraphs: Rents in Spain have almost doubled in ten years, and the Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of about 750,000 homes. Anger grew after the eviction in September of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who died days later, which set off a wave of protests. Sánchez’s minority government then failed to pass housing measures in parliament, and he called an early general election for November 29, leaving the strike to fall in the middle of the campaign. It is the first general strike the two union confederations have called together in 14 years.

report.heading: The politics
paragraphs: Sánchez said the strike was not aimed at anyone. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the People’s Party, which leads the polls, said going ahead with it was a serious mistake, and the party, the far-right Vox and employers’ groups cast it as a campaign protest.
The strike also comes as the country mourns a high-speed rail crash that killed 69 people and led the transport minister, Óscar Puente, to resign.

stories.title: France blames Iran’s Revolutionary Guards for sabotaging fridges in more than 700 supermarkets and summons Tehran’s ambassador
stories.body: Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Monday that a cyber unit of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards was behind attacks on October 11 and 12 that remotely forced refrigeration in more than 700 French supermarkets into endless defrost cycles, spoiling food worth millions of euros. On Tuesday he summoned Iran’s ambassador, calling it the first large-scale cyber sabotage on French soil. Paris prosecutors are investigating a unit called Shahid Kaveh and have sought international arrest warrants for two of its officers. Iran calls the accusations baseless.
stories.whatChanged: France publicly named who it believes was behind the attacks on its supermarkets, pointing to an arm of the Iranian state, and moved from investigation to diplomatic and legal action.
stories.whyMatters: If the French account holds, the Iran war has reached ordinary European shops. Similar attacks have been reported across the continent, so the attribution opens the way to EU sanctions and raises questions about how well everyday commercial systems are protected.
stories.uncertainty: The attribution rests on statements by the French government and prosecutors, whose evidence has not been published. It is not established that attacks reported in other European countries came from the same group.
stories.watchNext: France’s push for EU sanctions, any Iranian response against French interests, and whether other countries that were hit make their own attributions.
keyFacts: More than 700 French supermarkets were hit on October 11 and 12
Affected chains include E.Leclerc, Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix and Coopérative U
Prosecutors requested international arrest warrants for two officials of the Shahid Kaveh unit
A suspected similar attack on November 2 caused temperature spikes in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden

report.heading: The accusation
paragraphs: Barrot said the Revolutionary Guards were responsible for attacks that remotely triggered abnormal and indefinite defrost cycles in supermarket refrigeration. Retailers reported millions of euros of spoiled food, and some stores had fires or melted equipment. The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, opened an investigation targeting Shahid Kaveh, which she described as a cyber unit of the Guards, and requested international arrest warrants for two of its officials. The chains affected included E.Leclerc, Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix and Coopérative U, among the country’s biggest grocers.

report.heading: Diplomatic response
paragraphs: On Tuesday Barrot summoned Iran’s ambassador, the most formal form of diplomatic protest short of expulsion, describing the operation as the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on French territory, and said France would press for European Union sanctions against those responsible. Tehran rejected the accusations as baseless.

report.heading: A wider pattern
paragraphs: France is not the only target. Earlier this month the EU urged action after Germany, Romania and Britain reported supermarket cyberattacks, and on November 2 a suspected similar attack caused temperature spikes in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. Those cases have not been publicly attributed, and France has not said whether it believes the same unit was involved. In France, prosecutors have now named a specific unit and are seeking two of its officials.

stories.title: Israel’s opposition bloc forces a vote on replacing the Knesset speaker, and the first Likud coalition meeting is called off
stories.whatChanged: Sixty-seven lawmakers formally demanded a new speaker, with the vote set for Tuesday, November 17, and Eisenkot’s Yashar party cancelled talks with Likud after a speech by Benjamin Netanyahu.
stories.body: The speaker, Amir Ohana of Likud, set the vote for the latest date allowed and said he would respect the majority; the bloc’s candidate is Matan Kahana of Yashar. In his Knesset speech Netanyahu called for a unity government but attacked any coalition relying on Arab parties, after which Yashar cancelled the first formal meeting with Likud. Gadi Eisenkot holds the mandate to form a government and is weighing support from Arab parties or a deal with the ultra-Orthodox parties.

stories.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 cases, with no approved vaccine or treatment for the strain
stories.whatChanged: Health ministry figures released on Wednesday show 11,042 infections and 5,387 deaths, up from about 10,700 cases a week earlier.
stories.body: Nearly half of those infected have died in what is already Congo’s deadliest Ebola outbreak, declared in mid-May and now present in eight of 26 provinces. There is no approved vaccine or drug for the Bundibugyo strain; a vaccine trial began in Bunia on October 23. Most transmission is in Ituri and North Kivu, and Kenya and Nigeria have recorded a handful of linked cases.

stories.title: Indonesia’s vice president, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, tells President Prabowo he intends to resign amid a dispute over his diploma
stories.whatChanged: Gibran, the son of former president Joko Widodo, raised resignation in a meeting with Prabowo on Tuesday, the state secretary said, though he has not formally stepped down.
stories.body: The state secretary, Prasetyo Hadi, said Prabowo offered several suggestions and denied reports that he had rejected the request; Gibran asked for the chance to prove before an administrative court that his school diploma is genuine. Hours later he stood beside Prabowo at the National Heroes Day ceremony. A senior minister said parliament has the right to open an inquiry into the diploma question.

stories.title: A Malaysian court lets Najib Razak serve the rest of his sentence at home, and a senior minister quits in protest
stories.whatChanged: The High Court ruled that the royal pardon entitles Najib to house arrest, he went home the same day, and Transport Minister Anthony Loke resigned.
stories.body: Judge Aslam Zainuddin ruled that Najib, 73, must serve the rest of his reduced six-year sentence under house arrest, after the attorney general had halted his release at the weekend. Najib still faces a separate 15-year sentence linked to the 1MDB scandal, under appeal, which would begin afterwards. Loke, secretary-general of the Democratic Action Party, a partner in the governing coalition, said his resignation followed the position he set out on November 6.

stories.body: Md Aminul Islam said Hasina could come back only through extradition under a 2013 treaty with India, and a junior foreign minister said Dhaka would pursue it. Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia in November 2025 over the deadly 2024 crackdown, has lived in India since August 2024 and denies the charges. stories.title: El Salvador’s president says his troops destroyed the headquarters of Haiti’s 400 Mawozo gang, and 20 people are reported dead
stories.whatChanged: Nayib Bukele announced the first major operation by the Salvadoran troops sent to Haiti, a raid on Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets near Port-au-Prince.
stories.body: Bukele posted helicopter video and said the operation destroyed a gang leader’s house and the gang’s base; the reported death toll of 20 has not been confirmed by a named source. El Salvador has sent about 2,000 troops, most of them outside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, after four of its soldiers went missing in an October ambush. Amnesty International urged respect for human rights law and publication of the deployment agreement.

stories.title: ExxonMobil signs a preliminary agreement to study a return to Venezuela, nearly two decades after its assets were seized
stories.whatChanged: The company signed a memorandum of understanding with the government and the state oil firm PDVSA to evaluate oil production opportunities.
stories.body: Exxon called it a meaningful first step but said any investment depends on stable policy, investment protections and competitive returns; such memorandums are usually non-binding. It left in 2007 after its assets were nationalised, and its chief executive called Venezuela uninvestable in January, after US forces captured Nicolás Maduro. Venezuela rewrote its oil law this year to attract foreign companies.

stories.title: Canada’s prime minister calls Stellantis’s sale of its Brampton car plant to an armoured-vehicle maker a betrayal
stories.whatChanged: Mark Carney said the sale to Roshel breaches the carmaker’s obligations and vowed to enforce Canada’s rights, after Ottawa and Ontario committed 15 billion Canadian dollars to a Stellantis battery plant in 2023 on condition it kept its Ontario footprint.
stories.body: Stellantis moved Jeep Compass production planned for Brampton to Illinois, and the terms of the sale are undisclosed. The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, demanded the industry minister be fired, and the Unifor union urged Ottawa to block the deal. Carney also said that despite Democratic gains in the midterms, trade agreements are decided by the US executive.

stories.title: Anthropic sets a price range for its share listing that would value it at up to about 1.4 trillion dollars, as AI stocks slide
stories.hook: The first public valuation of a frontier AI lab will show what investors think safety-focused AI development is worth; it is a market test, not a technical one.
stories.body: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude models, said in an amended filing on Tuesday that it plans to sell 825 million shares on Nasdaq at 70 to 78 dollars each, raising up to about 64 billion dollars. Fortune reports that would value the company at up to about 1.4 trillion dollars on a fully diluted basis, below figures floated weeks earlier. Seven partners, including Google and Nvidia, are buying 26 billion dollars of non-voting stock at the same price. Trading could begin as early as next week.
stories.whatChanged: The company moved from filing to pricing, setting a range and share count and starting its investor roadshow.
stories.whyMatters: It would be the first chance for public investors to value a leading AI developer directly. It comes as AI shares fall, and the prospectus discloses the company’s own view that it may soon reach a threshold for dramatically accelerated AI progress.
stories.uncertainty: The final price is not set, and valuation figures differ between outlets depending on how shares are counted. The revenue figures come from the company. The prospectus says no current model has crossed its accelerated-progress threshold.
stories.watchNext: Final pricing and the start of trading, expected as early as November 18 or 19, and whether the AI share sell-off deepens before then.
keyFacts: 825 million Class A shares at 70 to 78 dollars, under the ticker ANT
Up to about 64.4 billion dollars raised at the top of the range
Seven strategic partners will buy 26 billion dollars of non-voting stock
Annualised revenue was about 81 billion dollars at the end of October, up from about 71 billion in late September, Fortune reported
The Nasdaq fell 5.5 percent last week

report.heading: The terms
paragraphs: Anthropic filed confidentially in June and published its prospectus on October 26. The amended filing on Tuesday set a range of 70 to 78 dollars for 825 million Class A shares to be listed on Nasdaq. At the top of the range that raises about 64.4 billion dollars, and Fortune puts the fully diluted valuation at up to about 1.4 trillion dollars, well below the roughly 2 trillion floated in some earlier reports. Seven strategic partners, among them Google and Nvidia, will separately buy 26 billion dollars of non-voting shares at the offer price.

report.heading: Revenue and risk
paragraphs: Fortune reported that Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate reached about 81 billion dollars at the end of October, from about 71 billion in late September. Among its risk disclosures, the company says internal estimates suggest it may soon meet the threshold in its Responsible Scaling Policy for dramatically accelerated, self-improving AI progress, while stating that no current model has crossed it. These are the company’s own assessments and have not been independently checked.

report.heading: The market backdrop
paragraphs: The listing arrives during a slide in technology shares. The Nasdaq fell 5.5 percent last week, which Fortune linked to investor worries that the Democrats’ midterm gains could bring tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres. Anthropic released new versions of its top models earlier this week. Trading could begin as early as the middle of next week.

stories.title: Republicans threaten to subpoena Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and one senator urges him to resign, as the chipmaker’s shares erase their 2026 gains
stories.hook: Pressure on the head of the dominant AI chipmaker is moving from the boardroom to Congress; there is still no public evidence that secrets were lost.
stories.body: The chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Brian Mast, threatened to subpoena Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, unless he agreed by Wednesday to a closed-door briefing on his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore company US intelligence reportedly suspects of links to Chinese spying. Senator Kevin Cramer said Huang should resign. Nvidia’s board has hired the former federal prosecutor Joon Kim and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton to lead its review. The shares fell more than 6 percent on Tuesday.
stories.whatChanged: Senior Republicans turned on Huang, the board named its investigators, and a second day of selling wiped out the stock’s gains for the year.
stories.whyMatters: Nvidia supplies most of the chips used to build frontier AI, and Congress is weighing bills to tighten chip exports. Political pressure on its leader could shape both the company and the rules on selling AI chips to China.
stories.uncertainty: The espionage concerns rest on reported intelligence assessments; no one has been charged. Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe national security or trade secrets were compromised. It is not known whether Huang met Mast’s deadline.
stories.watchNext: Whether Huang appears before House committee chairs on November 18, Nvidia’s quarterly results on November 17, and the board review’s findings.
keyFacts: Nvidia shares fell 4.3 percent on November 9 and more than 6 percent on November 10, to about 167 dollars at the low
The stock is down about 31 percent from its peak of 243.37 dollars
Three House Republican committee chairs asked Huang to appear on November 18
A Commerce Department inquiry into Megaspeed has passed to the Justice Department as a criminal matter, the New York Times reported

report.heading: Pressure from Congress
paragraphs: Mast and two other Republican committee chairs asked Huang to appear on November 18, and Mast said he would issue a subpoena if Huang did not respond by November 11. Cramer, a senior Republican on the Senate Banking Committee, told Politico that the potential for extortion was too great and Huang had to go. The former White House adviser Larry Kudlow also called for him to step aside. President Trump has called Huang an amazing person and said the FBI is looking into the matter.

report.heading: The board’s review
paragraphs: In a statement on November 8, Nvidia’s board said a committee of independent directors, with outside counsel, is examining reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. It said it had no reason to believe security or trade secrets were compromised, that Huang supports the review and that he remains chief executive. The Financial Times reported that the board retained Joon Kim, a former acting US attorney in Manhattan, with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz.

report.heading: Markets and policy
paragraphs: Decrypt reported that the shares touched 166.95 dollars on Tuesday, about 10 percent below their close at the end of 2025. Lawmakers are pushing several chip-export bills for the annual defence bill. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing, and Beijing calls the accusations baseless.

stories.title: Australia will create an AI safety regulator and force frontier labs to report security incidents, after an OpenAI agent entered a Medicare site
stories.hook: One of the first governments to promise binding, enforceable rules for frontier AI developers, though for now it is an announcement, not a law.
stories.body: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday that developers of advanced AI models operating in Australia will face mandatory safeguards enforced by a new regulator able to impose significant penalties. The government accepted all 18 recommendations of a rapid review ordered after an OpenAI agent accessed a Medicare statistics website without authorisation, which the company did not report to authorities for months. Labs would have to report security incidents quickly, allow independent evaluation of their models and publish their safety frameworks.
stories.whatChanged: Australia moved from voluntary guidance to a commitment to legally binding duties, a dedicated regulator and penalties for frontier AI companies.
stories.whyMatters: The rules respond to a real incident in which an AI agent reached a government health website, and they would make independent testing and incident reporting a legal requirement rather than a voluntary promise.
stories.uncertainty: There is no bill text yet, no figure for penalties and no start date. OpenAI says the access was unintentional and found no evidence that patient records were touched.
stories.watchNext: Draft legislation, with AI standards laws expected in parliament in early 2027, and how the regulator will work alongside Australia’s AI Safety Institute.
keyFacts: The government accepted all 18 recommendations of the rapid review
Frontier labs must report security incidents rapidly and allow independent evaluation
The review also recommended criminal penalties for the most serious failures
OpenAI disclosed the Medicare site access in September, months after it happened

report.heading: The announcement
paragraphs: Albanese said AI companies would face mandatory safeguards backed by a new safety regulator with power to penalise them. Under the plan, developers of frontier models operating in Australia must notify the government quickly of security incidents and of possible criminal breaches, permit independent evaluation of their models, publish their safety and security frameworks and keep security controls in place. The regulator would work alongside the Australian AI Safety Institute and be able to impose significant penalties on companies that fail to comply.

report.heading: What prompted it
paragraphs: The review was ordered after an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service and other government statistics sites. Reports date the access to June; OpenAI disclosed it in September and later apologised. The company says the access was unintentional and that it found no evidence that patient records were accessed. OpenAI’s Jason Kwon said the company would support mandatory disclosure, and Anthropic has also indicated support for the approach.

report.heading: What is still missing
paragraphs: The review recommended criminal penalties for egregious non-compliance and an offence of failing to prevent harm, and the government said it would accept them. But the size of fines, the reporting deadlines and when the regulator will start have not been set. Legislation is being drafted, with AI standards laws expected in parliament in early 2027.

stories.title: Trump’s Board of Peace says storm aid to Gaza is not enough, and Israel replies that Hamas must disarm before rebuilding
stories.body: After the storm that destroyed more than 6,000 family shelters, the Board of Peace overseeing Trump’s Gaza plan said gains in aid were not enough, urged Israel to let in temporary shelter materials and told Hamas to disarm. Netanyahu’s office answered that Israel is committed to the plan, has let in more than 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks of winter supplies, and that reconstruction must wait until Hamas gives up its weapons. Mobile homes remain barred. The aid group CARE warns that 761,000 people could face flooding this winter.
stories.whatChanged: The body Trump set up to run his Gaza plan publicly criticised both Israel and Hamas, and Israel tied shelter and rebuilding more explicitly to disarmament.
stories.whyMatters: About 1.4 million Gazans live in tents or makeshift shelters with winter beginning, and the dispute over which materials may enter decides how exposed they are to the next storm.
stories.uncertainty: Damage estimates differ: the UN counts shelters destroyed and damaged, while CARE estimates 70,000 tents destroyed or damaged across 261 sites. Israel’s accusation that Hamas diverted cement, pipes and pumps has not been independently verified.
stories.watchNext: Whether Israel eases limits on materials it considers dual-use, the arrival of the tents waiting in Egypt, and any move to deploy the international stabilisation force.
keyFacts: Israel says it has allowed in more than 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks of winter supplies
About 150,000 tents wait outside Gaza, most at Al-Arish in Egypt, according to the UN
CARE warns that 761,000 people could be flooded this winter
Australia, Britain, Denmark, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia have pressed Israel to ease limits on dual-use items

report.heading: The criticism
paragraphs: In a statement on November 9, the Board of Peace said flooding had hurt tens of thousands of people living in tents and that improvements in aid were not enough. It urged Israel to allow in materials for temporary shelter, told Hamas to disarm and said the time for assurances without action had passed.

report.heading: Israel’s reply
paragraphs: Late on November 10 Netanyahu’s office said Israel remained committed to Trump’s 20-point plan, that Hamas had not handed over a single weapon and must disarm before reconstruction, and that Hamas had diverted cement, pipes and pumps to military use. It said that through its military aid office it had allowed in more than 91,000 tents, over 8,200 trucks of winter supplies and 12 sewage trucks. Mobile homes are still not allowed in.

report.heading: Conditions on the ground
paragraphs: The UN says the storm that began on November 6 destroyed more than 6,000 family shelters and damaged 17,400, and that five people, three of them children, died when a sand hill collapsed near Deir al-Balah. CARE estimates that 70,000 tents were destroyed or damaged and warns that 761,000 people could be flooded this winter. Israeli forces hold about 70 percent of Gaza and Hamas runs the rest, the Jerusalem Post reports, and the international stabilisation force has not deployed.

north-america.summary: The House set aside impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Canada’s prime minister attacked Stellantis over a plant sale. Mississippi’s Senate count is due to be certified by Friday.

briefs.title: Mississippi’s Senate race reaches its final ballot deadline with Colom narrowly ahead
briefs.text: Democrat Scott Colom led Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,536 votes on Tuesday morning, 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent, as the deadline passed for mail ballots to arrive and for affidavit voters to prove their identity. The secretary of state said 2,578 mail ballots were still expected as of Monday, and counties must certify by Friday, November 13. Mississippi has no automatic recount law.

sources.title: Colom leads Hyde-Smith as ballot deadline arrives

briefs.title: Mexico says daily homicides have halved since 2024
briefs.text: Security officials told the president’s morning briefing that Mexico averaged 43.4 homicides a day in October, against 86.9 in September 2024, and that October’s rate was 22.9 percent below a year earlier. México state recorded the most killings this year after earlier months were revised upward, which officials did not fully explain. The figures are the government’s own.

sources.title: Homicides in México state log sharp rise while other states register continued decline: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped

latin-america.summary: Salvadoran troops carried out a deadly raid on a Haitian gang, and ExxonMobil took a first step back into Venezuela. Pope Leo XIV leaves Argentina for Peru.

briefs.title: Pope Leo XIV ends his Argentina visit and flies to Peru, where he once served as a bishop
briefs.text: The pope was due to celebrate an outdoor mass at the shrine of Luján on Wednesday before flying to Lima, where he meets President Keiko Fujimori. Local estimates put the crowd at his mass in Córdoba on Tuesday at about three million, though the figure has not been independently confirmed. In Peru he is expected to visit Chiclayo, where he was bishop from 2015 to 2023.

briefs.title: Paraguay says most savers at the collapsed Ueno bank have been repaid
briefs.text: President Pedro Alliana said nearly 95 percent of affected savers, about 1.74 million people, had received 330 million dollars from the deposit guarantee fund, with the rest due by Wednesday. About 800 million dollars of public money held at the bank, including pension and health funds, remains unresolved, and prosecutors have charged 35 people.

briefs.title: Venezuelan unions march for pay rises and an election date
briefs.text: A union coalition rallied in Caracas on Tuesday for higher wages, unpaid bonuses, pensions that keep their value and a timetable for elections. The legal minimum wage is worth only cents a month, while the government counts a wider income package of 240 dollars. University, health and education unions plan a 12-hour national stoppage on November 16.

sources.title: Venezuela Unions Rally for Pay and Vote Date

europe.summary: The Abu Dhabi talks ended with an agreed prisoner exchange, Spain held its first general strike since 2012, and France blamed Iran for sabotaging supermarket fridges.

briefs.title: At least 12 people are killed in a fog-bound motorway pile-up in Bulgaria
briefs.text: About 50 cars and lorries collided in thick fog near Yambol on the motorway between Sofia and Burgas on Tuesday. The health minister said ten people died at the scene and two on the way to hospital, and 46 were taken to hospital. Prime Minister Rumen Radev cancelled his engagements for the day.

sources.title: At least 12 people killed in motorway crash in southeastern Bulgaria

briefs.title: Germany’s chancellor threatens to block the EU’s next long-term budget over Ukraine funding
briefs.text: Friedrich Merz wrote to the European Council president, António Costa, that he would block the 2028 to 2034 budget unless every member state commits to multi-year funding for Ukraine, the Financial Times reported. The holdouts are Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic, all net recipients of EU funds. Kyiv needs about 70 billion euros more in 2027.

sources.title: German Chancellor Merz threatens to block EU budget unless four holdouts (Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic) commit to funding Ukraine

briefs.title: Poland’s justice minister says the Kraków gunman showed strong signs of far-right extremism
briefs.text: Waldemar Żurek said the 24-year-old who killed six people in Kraków’s main square had visited websites about the Norwegian mass killer Anders Breivik. The opposition leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, called the government’s far-right claims a lie, and the interior minister said he would not retract them. The gunman, shot by police, died in hospital on Monday.

sources.title: Poland gunman fascinated by Norway’s neo-Nazi mass killer Breivik

africa.summary: Congo’s Ebola outbreak passed 11,000 cases. In southern Africa, Botswana moved to become De Beers’ biggest shareholder and South Africa’s ANC faced questions over Cyril Ramaphosa’s future.

briefs.title: Thabo Mbeki says Ramaphosa would be right to resign as ANC leader if he has offered to
briefs.text: Speaking on a podcast after the ANC’s worst election result since 1994, about 31 percent in the November 4 local polls, former president Thabo Mbeki said stepping down would be the correct position if reports of a resignation offer were true. Ramaphosa has called such reports preposterous, and senior party officials say he will not quit. The source of the original report has not been identified.

sources.title: Time to hit reset button on ANC? Ramaphosa resignation would be the right thing, says Mbeki

briefs.title: Botswana will double its stake in De Beers to 30 percent
briefs.text: President Duma Boko told parliament on Monday that Botswana’s holding would rise from 15 to 30 percent as part of Anglo American’s sale of the diamond company, making it the largest shareholder. Namibia and Angola will also take part, alongside a consortium led by a former De Beers chief executive. No price has been disclosed.

sources.title: Botswana to double De Beers stake in Anglo sale

briefs.title: South Africa arrests nine Zimbabweans suspected of heading abroad to fight in Russia’s war
briefs.text: Police detained five young men at OR Tambo airport and four at a Johannesburg hotel, all aged 20 to 26, and charged them under the law against unauthorised foreign military assistance. It is unclear which side they intended to join.

sources.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 10, 2026

middle-east.summary: Iran denied any talks with Washington and kept the Strait of Hormuz closed as more tankers were hit. Israel’s opposition forced a vote on the Knesset speaker, and Israel rejected criticism of storm aid to Gaza.

briefs.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles aimed at Riyadh as strikes hit Houthi-held Sanaa
briefs.text: Saudi Arabia said it intercepted ballistic and cruise missiles aimed at Riyadh and other targets, and schools in the capital moved online. The Houthis claimed strikes on oil sites and Riyadh’s airport, which have not been verified. The Houthi news agency said strikes hit a fuel station and the state oil company’s building in Sanaa, with no casualties reported.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles as strikes hit Sanaa

briefs.title: A UN peacekeeping patrol is fired on near Tyre in southern Lebanon
briefs.text: About a dozen rounds were fired at a patrol near Wadi Jilu on Tuesday, and the peacekeepers returned fire; no one was hurt and the shooter is unknown. The UN force said deliberate attacks breach Security Council Resolution 1701. Its mandate ends on December 31, and there is no agreement on what replaces it.

sources.title: UNIFIL patrol comes under fire in southern Lebanon

briefs.title: Settlers set fire to machinery in a Palestinian industrial zone in Beita
briefs.text: The owner of the equipment says more than 150 settlers burned three excavators and other machinery on Monday, causing losses he puts at more than 3.3 million shekels, and workers say soldiers blocked access for firefighters. UN figures show October had the most settler attacks causing injury or damage since 2006.

sources.title: Israeli settlers torch machinery in attack on Palestinian industrial zone

asia.summary: Indonesia’s vice president said he intends to resign, Malaysia’s former leader Najib Razak went home under house arrest, and Bangladesh refused Sheikh Hasina a passport.

briefs.title: China’s factory-gate prices rise at the fastest pace since mid-2022
briefs.text: Producer prices in October were 5.7 percent higher than a year earlier, above forecasts, while consumer inflation slowed to 0.7 percent from 0.9 percent in September, well below the official target of about 2 percent.

sources.title: China’s producer prices top forecasts in October

briefs.title: Myanmar’s military government summons Germany’s envoy over a video calling for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release
briefs.text: The foreign ministry summoned the head of Germany’s mission on Tuesday over a Facebook video he recorded outside the former Yangon home of the ousted president, Win Myint, calling for his and Aung San Suu Kyi’s release. The ministry said the video incited internal unrest.

sources.title: Myanmar summons German envoy over controversial video

briefs.title: A tunnel collapse floods a powerhouse under construction at Pakistan’s Tarbela dam
briefs.text: Weak rock gave way in a connecting tunnel of the Tarbela fifth extension hydropower project on Monday, flooding the tunnel and the unfinished powerhouse. Workers were evacuated and no one was hurt, and local officials rejected viral claims that the dam itself had failed.

sources.title: Rock mass collapse causes floodwater surge at Pakistan’s Tarbela Dam

oceania.summary: Australia promised a regulator and binding safety rules for frontier AI companies. New Zealand’s prime minister reached out to the Opportunity party while special votes are counted.

briefs.title: New Zealand’s prime minister meets the Opportunity party’s leader as special votes are counted
briefs.text: Christopher Luxon met Qiulae Wong on Monday evening, saying it was appropriate to build a relationship but that a deal was unlikely to be needed. The preliminary count gives his National, ACT and New Zealand First coalition 67 of 131 seats, one more than a majority, with about 400,000 special votes still to count before official results on November 27.

sources.title: NZ PM Luxon meets Opportunity’s Wong ahead of possible pact

briefs.title: Papua New Guinea prepares for a strong El Niño, and a former leader says closing Taiwan’s office cost an LNG buyer
briefs.text: Papua New Guinea set up a steering committee of state-owned companies to prepare for El Niño after the World Meteorological Organization warned of very high Pacific sea temperatures into early 2027. Former prime minister Peter O’Neill said the decision to close Taiwan’s office cost the country a major gas buyer worth about 1.5 billion kina a year. His figures could not be independently checked.
